items.why: Consent and Paul’s transfer are both plausible prerequisites; “before the ambushers act” does not clearly specify the step sought.
The rescue context clearly identifies the slain Philistine as Ishbi-Benob, not David.
“Gives the message” could mean the father’s current report or the buried man’s earlier declaration.
Readers must distinguish the leaders commanding the army from the officials who muster it.
The refusal has a clear reason, but the key omits what God commanded him not to do.
The sequence clearly distinguishes the noise that draws Athaliah there from what she sees afterward.
Readers can connect reverence with “fear of God” and clearly identify Zechariah as the teacher.
The two covenants have clearly different participants, making the first agreement identifiable.
“Are all to guard the temple” includes both sets of companies, not only the two named in the key.
The prediction and its fulfillment clearly connect the final “him” to the officer.
The key “the news” never states what was reported and rewards repeating a vague label.
Readers must distinguish Jehoiada, who distributes the weapons, from David, their former owner.
The final sentence supplies the collective answer, though only one of the four is described here.
The king sends the messenger, allowing readers to identify the person Elisha calls a murderer.
This mostly tests which killer is mentioned first; the separate battles do not establish a first killing.
The letter heading clearly distinguishes its sender from its recipient without requiring prior knowledge.
Readers must connect the predicted son Josiah with the later “he” who sacrifices the priests.
The next step is clear, but the question presents the king’s imagined enemy plan as established intention.
“Addressee” is needlessly technical, though the final sentence clearly identifies the accusers.
The warning clearly targets the man from Judah, but “whose body is warned” is awkward wording.
The men’s reasoning clearly distinguishes their chosen chance of survival from the rejected options.
Tracking the attacker and the beaten men clearly identifies Sceva’s sons as those who flee.
The quoted fear distinguishes the expected attackers from the king believed to have hired them.
Readers must distinguish the soldiers returning from the cavalry continuing with Paul.
The king’s reaction clearly makes the man of God the target of “Seize him!”
The answer simply repeats the opening negative statement, requiring little interpretation.
The return and report are clearly placed between the scouting trip and the plundering.
The men’s decision to share the discovery clearly follows their admission that keeping it secret is wrong.
The order is addressed to the two centurions, not to the soldiers they must assemble.
The reply is identifiable, but the key leaves both the officer and the promised food implicit.
Paul clearly assigns the message to the young man, also identifiable as his nephew.
The passage distinguishes three military opponents from the Ammonites who pay tribute.
The causal link is clear, though “whose love of soil” sounds unnecessarily tied to the excerpt’s wording.
“Him” clearly refers to Uzziah, although the later confrontation makes the answer especially easy.
The claimed instruction clearly identifies the man of God as the person to be brought back for a meal.
Readers can connect “interceded” with the requested prayer and distinguish the helper from the king.
It asks only for the first action in a short list rather than understanding the siege or famine.
The succession is explicit, but answering mainly requires repeating the next sentence.
Following the pronouns from the father’s request identifies the old prophet, not his sons.
Readers must connect the departing “he” to the man for whom the donkey was saddled.
Paul’s planned departure the next day clearly explains his unusually long speech.
Tracking “my son” in the woman’s account distinguishes the child eaten from the child hidden.
Talking until daylight is clearly the last action before departure, after the meal.
The passage explicitly connects the city’s calm with Athaliah’s death.
“Assembling materials” disguises bringing scrolls together and makes a simple sequence unnecessarily opaque.
The cause is clear, though the key leaves the concrete affliction—leprosy—unstated.
The gate assignment anchors “him” to the officer despite the intervening mention of the king.
The surrounding orders also imply the woman’s execution, making her a reasonable answer too.
Tracking the quoted speaker’s “my son” establishes tomorrow as the day for the other woman’s child.
The city and tomb are overlapping destinations, making “first” an artificial distinction within one return trip.
Illnesses also disappear through healing, so excluding them relies on matching “leaves” rather than understanding.
“Ahaziah’s son’s nurse” creates a needless relationship puzzle when the passage plainly names Joash.
The purpose is explicit, though the question mostly restates the opening sentence using a family label.
The plan distinguishes the commander who brings Paul from the council requesting his appearance.
